excerpt: an employer that forbears from terminating an existing at-will employee forbears from exercising a legal right, and that therefore such forbearance constitutes adequate consideration for a noncompetition agreement
note: Lucht's Concrete Pumping v. Horner, 255 P.3d 1058 (Colo. 2011), opinion text via Caselaw Access Project (Justia/CourtListener returned 403/empty to WebFetch). The 2022 amendments to C.R.S. 8-2-113 add notice and compensation-threshold requirements; I did not find any text in them that overrules Lucht on consideration. That point was not checked against the statute text directly.

excerpt: the continuation of plaintiffs employment for approximately three years after he signed the letter which acknowledges the covenant also provides consideration for the restrictive covenant
note: Hogan v. Bergen Brunswig Corp., 153 N.J. Super. 37 (App. Div. 1977), reversing the trial court's finding of no consideration. This is an intermediate appellate decision, and the NJ Supreme Court has not squarely held the point.

excerpt: an employer's promise to continue at will employment is valid consideration for the employee's promise not to compete with the employer after his termination.
note: Ackerman v. Kimball Int'l, 652 N.E.2d 507 (Ind. 1995). The employee signed after 11 years of at-will employment.

excerpt: continuing employment for an indefinite period is sufficient consideration to support a covenant not to compete.
note: Farm Bureau Serv. Co. of Maynard v. Kohls, 203 N.W.2d 209 (Iowa 1972). The covenant was signed about two months after employment began.

excerpt: the continuation of employment for a substantial period beyond the threat of discharge is sufficient consideration for a restrictive covenant.
note: Simko, Inc. v. Graymar Co., 55 Md. App. 561 (1983). Qualification: consideration fails if the employer discharges the employee without cause within an unconscionably short time, or bargains in bad faith. So the answer is yes, subject to a 'substantial period' condition, not unconditionally.
